newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Mandela in Congo to host shipborne Zaire talks.
newsitem.headline: Mandela in Congo to host shipborne Zaire talks.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela arrived in Congo on Wednesday for last-chance talks to unite Zaire's President Mobutu Sese Seko and rebel leader Laurent Kabila on a peace plan.

Mobutu and Kabila were scheduled to meet face-to-face for the second time on South African navy icebreaker Outeniqua off Congo's port of Pointe Noire to discuss a transition to democracy after 32 years of autocratic rule by Mobutu.

Kabila, whose forces have been closing in on Zaire's capital Kinshasa, has been insisting, in public at least, that Mobutu must stand down on Wednesday if he wants to avert a bloody battle for the city.
He was due to arrive in Pointe Noire by helicopter from the nearby port of Soyo in Angola, sources close to the talks said.

Witnesses in Kinshasa, unusually quiet after an overnight curfew and an opposition stay-at-home protest call, said Mobutu's motorcade went to the international airport. Access was restricted, preventing formal confirmation of his departure.
Zairean state radio said that Wednesday would be a fateful day that could determine the future of Africa's third largest and potentially one of its richest countries.
Mediators have expressed optimism over the talks.
"President Mandela and Deputy President (Thabo) Mbeki are both quite optimistic that an agreement can be reached on Wednesday," Mandela spokesman Joel Netshitenzhe said earlier.
He spokes of an agreement being reached by telephone on Tuesday on the framework for an accord.
U.S. special envoy Bill Richardson, who helped bring Mobutu and Kabila together for an inconclusive meeting on the ship on May 4, shared the South African optimism.

"I am optimistic that there will be a soft landing and a peaceful, inclusive transition, mainly because of South Africa's very strong and effective and skilful efforts," he told reporters at the United Nations in New York.
Mobutu, 66 and suffering from cancer, has dominated Zaire since seizing power in 1965, reputedly amassing a huge personal fortune.
The rebels, who took up arms in October demanding Zairean nationality for ethnic Tutsis, now control three-quarters of the impoverished, corruption-plagued nation.
Kabila and his spokesmen have said throughout the peace talks that Mobutu must hand power to them. They have ruled out a transfer of power to any other transitional authority.
Reports reaching Kinshasa on Tuesday said the rebels had taken the key bridge over the River Kwango and Mobutu's army had pulled back to Mbankana about 150 km (90 miles) from the city.
Information Minister Kin-Kiey Mulumba spoke on Monday of fierce fighting in the region of Kenge, 60 km (40 miles) to the east of the bridge.
Kabila's son Joseph, a frontline commander, said then that the rebels were advancing on all fronts.
The United States, one of a number of Western countries with troops in Congo to evacuate nationals from Kinshasa if need be, urged Kabila on Tuesday to be a responsible leader.

Kabila had "enormous authority over one of the most important countries in Africa... And we hope very much that he will be able to meet these tests," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters in Washington.
